title: Disability, Rights, Identity, and Belonging
before: How medical, social, cultural and rights-based views of disability shape identity, rights and belonging in DSD services and work.

turns.text: Disability, Rights, Identity, and Belonging asks DSD staff to understand disability through more than limitations. The course compares medical, social, cultural, and rights-based ways of understanding disability, and it looks at how each one shapes questions of identity, rights, and belonging, both in the services people receive and in the workplace we share.

It starts with two sentences about the same situation. “The person cannot complete our form” directs attention toward the person. “The form requires handwriting in small boxes” makes a design condition visible. The course asks what each description could lead the next reader to do, which is a useful question for almost anything we write.

That opening sets up the course’s different perspectives on disability. A medical view asks about a condition or treatment, while a social view asks what in the environment restricts participation. Functional, rights-based, cultural, and intersectional views add questions about activity, entitlement, identity, and interacting barriers. The course is clear that no single view describes the whole person, so each one answers a different question.

The first practice case is about public writing, where a program page describes people chiefly as unable to manage ordinary life and says staff decide what is best. The wording may obscure strengths, chosen support, and decision-making, and repetition can normalize low expectations. You will weigh revisions, and the course notes that required legal or program terms have their own review.

I appreciate that the course does not swing too far the other way. Removing barriers should not erase pain, fatigue, communication needs, or other experiences a person chooses to describe. The suggestion is to ask what helps with this activity rather than requesting unnecessary medical detail, while actual care and formal processes keep their own responsibilities.

The rights section draws a similar line between good intentions and what a process owes people. A rights-based view asks about access, equal opportunity, participation, and the responsibilities of the relevant process, which is more than a charitable response, however well meant. For actual rights, service, or accommodation questions, the course points staff to the responsible agency routes rather than a learning module.

Then there is disability as identity and culture. Disability communities include histories, languages, arts, humor, organizing, and varied views about access. Some people understand disability as central to who they are, and others describe it differently. That is also why the course treats person-first and identity-first language as preferences that belong to people, not as one universal rule.

The onboarding case will be familiar to some of us. A new employee asks for an accessible training format, and a colleague treats the request as a sign the role may not fit. That inference can turn a design gap into a capability judgment before the work has been examined. You will decide on the most useful response and see what each option could lead to.

Another case comes from a service-design session, where a disabled participant is asked for an inspiring personal story instead of comments on the form under review. The course explains how that request can replace practical expertise with a familiar narrative. It also describes interdependence: people commonly rely on relationships, tools, and shared knowledge, and using support does not remove agency.

Near the end, you rewrite a description without losing the need. You keep the relevant support need, restore the person’s agency, and name a condition that could change. The course also separates an immediate alternative from a design review that helps the next person, and it reminds us that reframing a sentence is a learning step, not a completed finding.

As you begin, think of a description you have read or written recently, perhaps in a note, a template, or a public page. Who does it present as the problem, and what does it leave out? You will not need any personal records. The course will help you keep the need, restore the person’s role, and find the condition that could be reviewed.

guidance.title: Different views, different questions
guidance.text: Each perspective on disability is a tool for a particular question. A medical view helps when the question is about a condition or treatment. A social view helps you see a barrier in the environment, and a rights-based view asks what the process owes the person. Choosing the lens that fits the question keeps you from mistaking one partial account for a description of the whole person.

guidance.title: What a later reader would understand
guidance.text: Look again at the description you rewrote. If a colleague read only your version months from now, what would they understand differently about the person and the barrier? What support need did you make sure to keep? Consider what evidence would show that a change actually helped, and what question would stay open until the people affected could tell you.
